task_row_model.query:
Let f_p(z) = sum_{n=1}^
fty z^n / n^p for complex z with |z|<=1 and real parameter p>0. Determine for which p and which points z on the unit circle the series converges. Prove that the sum defines an analytic function on the open unit disc. For points on |z|=1 where the series converges, discuss whether and when the sum admits analytic continuation across the boundary point. Provide rigorous arguments using standard tests (root/ratio, Abel, Dirichlet, etc.).

documents.content: The power series sum_{n=1}^∞ z^n / n^p has radius of convergence equal to 1. This follows from limsup_{n->∞} |a_n|^{1/n} = limsup n^{-p/n} = 1, so the series converges for |z|<1 and diverges for |z|>1. On any compact subset of the open unit disc, say |z|<=r<1, the terms satisfy |z|^n / n^p <= r^n / n^p and the tail is dominated by a convergent geometric factor; hence uniform convergence on compacta follows by comparison with a geometric series and the Weierstrass M-test. Termwise differentiation is therefore valid and the sum is holomorphic on |z|<1 for every p>0.
documents.reasoning_trace: I established radius of convergence by computing the root-limit of coefficients n^{-p}, then argued uniform convergence on compacta using comparison for |z|<=r<1 and the Weierstrass M-test. I invoked termwise differentiation to conclude holomorphicity on the open disc.

documents.content: Convergence properties of Fourier series often rely on kernels such as Fejér or Dirichlet kernels. If one considers partial sums of exp(i n theta) weighted by coefficients that decrease to zero, Cesaro summation can yield pointwise convergence even when the ordinary series fails. In particular, boundedness of partial sums of the exponential sequence and monotonic decay of coefficients are hypotheses in Dirichlet-type tests for trigonometric series. Equidistribution or cancellation of exponential sums plays a major role in controlling oscillatory behaviour of the partial sums and obtaining summability results.
documents.reasoning_trace: I summarized classical Fourier series techniques: kernel methods, Cesaro/Fejér summation, and the role of bounded partial sums and monotone coefficients in applying Dirichlet-type convergence tests.

For 0

1. If theta is not an integer multiple of 2pi then the partial sums S_N = sum_{n=1}^N e^{i n theta} are uniformly bounded (S_N = e^{i theta}(1-e^{i N theta})/(1-e^{i theta})), while the positive sequence 1/n^p decreases to 0 for p>0. Applying Dirichlet's test yields convergence for every p>0 when z on the circle but z ≠ 1. At z=-1 (theta=pi) this is the alternating p-series and converges for p>0 by the alternating test. Regarding analytic continuation, pointwise convergence at a boundary point does not automatically give a neighborhood where the sum extends holomorphically; analytic continuation across a boundary point requires absence of singularities on the circle and additional structure. In particular, while the series sums to a finite limit at many boundary points, whether a holomorphic extension exists beyond |z|=1 depends on global analytic continuation properties of the summed function and cannot be guaranteed purely from the termwise series convergence.
documents.reasoning_trace: I combined radius-of-convergence and Dirichlet test: computed boundedness of geometric partial sums for e^{i n theta}, noted monotone decay of 1/n^p, applied Dirichlet to get convergence for theta not 0, treated z=1 and z=-1 separately, and stated the standard distinction between pointwise boundary convergence and analytic continuation.

documents.content: At the specific boundary point z=1 the series becomes the classical p-series sum 1/n^p; convergence is equivalent to p>1 by integral-test comparison with the integral of x^{-p}. At z=-1 the series is alternating with general term 1/n^p decreasing to zero for p>0, so the alternating series test (Leibniz criterion) gives convergence for all p>0. These two special points illustrate that different points on the unit circle can have distinct convergence behavior depending on arithmetic cancellation. Many standard proofs for these cases use monotone decreasing of coefficients and direct comparison or alternating criteria.
documents.reasoning_trace: I focused on boundary-specific tests: used integral comparison to determine convergence at z=1, and used the alternating series test for z=-1, highlighting how monotone decay and sign cancellation produce convergence in those special cases.

documents.content: The Riemann zeta function extends the Dirichlet series sum_{n=1}^∞ 1/n^s meromorphically to the complex plane with a simple pole at s=1; its analytic continuation and functional equation are classical. Mellin transforms, Euler products and contour-shift methods are standard tools in establishing continuation and locating zeros. In particular, analytic continuation is obtained by expressing zeta(s) in terms of the Gamma function and a rapidly converging series or integral representation, then shifting contours and subtracting poles. These techniques are central in analytic number theory and in proofs of distribution results for primes.
documents.reasoning_trace: I outlined standard methods for analytic continuation of Dirichlet series like zeta(s): Mellin transforms, Gamma factors, contour integration and subtraction of the simple pole at s=1 to obtain a meromorphic extension.
